question: A 30-year-old man comes to the physician because of an episode of bloody vomiting this morning and a 1-week history of burning upper abdominal pain. Two weeks ago, he sustained a head injury and was in a coma for 3 days. An endoscopy shows multiple, shallow hemorrhagic lesions predominantly in the gastric fundus and greater curvature. Biopsies show patchy loss of epithelium and an acute inflammatory infiltrate in the lamina propria that does not extend beyond the muscularis mucosa. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "30-year-old man with bloody vomiting" -> "1-week history of burning upper abdominal pain" -> "recent head injury and coma" -> "endoscopy shows shallow hemorrhagic lesions" -> "biopsies show patchy loss of epithelium" -> "acute inflammatory infiltrate in lamina propria" -> "does not extend beyond muscularis mucosa" -> "consistent with erosive gastritis" -> 85%

CHAIN: "30-year-old man with bloody vomiting" -> "upper abdominal pain for 1 week" -> "head injury 2 weeks ago" -> "endoscopy reveals hemorrhagic lesions" -> "biopsy shows acute inflammation" -> "inflammation limited to lamina propria" -> "suggests erosive gastritis" -> 80%

CHAIN: "Patient has bloody vomiting" -> "burning upper abdominal pain present" -> "head injury history" -> "endoscopy shows shallow lesions" -> "biopsy indicates acute inflammation" -> "inflammation does not extend beyond muscularis mucosa" -> "Cushing ulcer possible but less likely" -> "erosive gastritis more likely" -> 75%

CHAIN: "Bloody vomiting and abdominal pain" -> "recent head trauma" -> "endoscopy shows shallow hemorrhagic lesions" -> "biopsy shows acute inflammatory infiltrate" -> "inflammation confined to lamina propria" -> "Cushing ulcer considered due to head injury" -> "erosive gastritis is more consistent with findings" -> 70%
analysis: The patient's presentation of bloody vomiting, burning upper abdominal pain, and endoscopic findings of multiple shallow hemorrhagic lesions in the gastric fundus and greater curvature, along with the acute inflammatory infiltrate, suggests erosive gastritis. The history of head injury and subsequent coma indicates a potential for stress-related mucosal disease, which can lead to erosive gastritis. Cushing ulcers are typically associated with increased intracranial pressure and are more likely to be deeper ulcers, while the other options do not fit the clinical picture as well as erosive gastritis.
